The shadowing 'let mut OldHeap = OldHeap;' was removed, which can change mutability and drop/timing semantics of OldHeap (affecting when its Drop runs and whether it could be mutated or disarmed), potentially altering resource cleanup behavior.

The conditional call to disarm_closer was removed so OldHeap's Drop will always run on the success path; if cluster_rel_body still performs the by-OID relation_close, this can double-release/double-close the relcache reference and cause a backend crash or memory-safety issue.

Relation::disarm_closer was removed, eliminating the intended escape hatch to suppress Drop-based relcache releases when another path has already closed the relation, increasing the risk of double-release/use-after-free if any callers perform manual by-OID closes.

The method reads routes_version once and then unconditionally rebuilds and assigns that stale routes_version to _effective_candidates_version; if original_router.routes changes during the rebuild the cache version can be set incorrectly, causing stale/incorrect cache results to be returned.
The code assigns self._effective_candidates = [] and then appends into it without synchronization, exposing a partially-built list to concurrent readers and causing inconsistent visible state.

effective_low_priority_routes() reads the routes version only once and then rebuilds and writes that (potentially stale) version back; concurrent modifications to original_router.routes during the rebuild can cause the stored version to be incorrect and the cache to be stale.

effective_low_priority_routes() mutates self._effective_low_priority_routes in-place without locking, which can expose a partially-populated list to concurrent callers and produce inconsistent results.

Using get_route_path(scope) and checking the route's final segment for an extension can inspect the route pattern (e.g. '/items/{path}') instead of the actual requested path, so requests for asset filenames routed through path parameters will be misclassified as frontend navigations.

Using os.path.splitext on the final path segment will not treat dotfiles (e.g. '.env', '.gitignore') as having an extension (splitext returns empty extension), so requests for such files may be incorrectly classified as navigations.

Changing behavior to treat '*/*' as indicating a frontend navigation (unless text/html is explicitly q=0) can cause requests with an absent Accept header or with a generic '*/*' to be classified as browser navigations whereas previously they were not; this alters semantics and may misclassify API/asset requests.

Changing to getattr(r, 'name', 'unknown') suppresses AttributeError that would previously surface when a route context lacked a name, masking configuration bugs and altering the error message content.

Replacing the AsyncExitStack-managed async context manager with an async generator that owns the task group can cause the producer task group to be cancelled during async generator finalization (GeneratorExit) rather than during structured teardown, reintroducing the original race/teardown ordering the prior code avoided.

After yielding KEEPALIVE_COMMENT on timeout the new generator does not perform the checkpoint await anyio.sleep(0) (previously applied to all yielded items), reducing cancellation responsiveness when a keepalive is yielded.

Removing the custom GenerateJsonSchema subclass (and replacing the local alias with pydantic.GenerateJsonSchema) can cause runtime failures or behavior changes on older/unsupported pydantic versions that lack the expected bytes_schema implementation.

Dropping the bytes_schema override removes logic that added contentEncoding (e.g., base64) depending on FastAPI/Pydantic configuration, changing the produced JSON schema for bytes and potentially producing inaccurate schemas for endpoints expecting contentMediaType/contentEncoding.

Changing UploadFile's JSON schema from contentMediaType to format: 'binary' drops contentMediaType/contentEncoding metadata consumers may rely on and may be incompatible with tools or code that expect contentMediaType to indicate the media type.

Assigning self.on_startup/self.on_shutdown before validating the prefix changes initialization side-effects so these attributes exist even if subsequent validation (assert) raises, leading to a partially-initialized object visible to exception handlers or finalizers.

Eagerly copying on_startup/on_shutdown iterables with list(...) may consume generator-based iterables earlier than before due to the reordering, changing when/if the original iterators can be iterated elsewhere.

Removing the Json-field special case causes sequence-typed fields annotated with pydantic.Json to be pulled with values.getlist, changing the input shape (multiple single JSON values vs. a single JSON string) and likely breaking JSON parsing/validation for those fields.

Dropping the annotation_format=Format.FORWARDREF fallback on NameError removes the mechanism that avoided evaluating TYPE_CHECKING-only forward-reference annotations on Python >=3.14, which can reintroduce NameError (runtime crash) when calling inspect.signature.

Removing param.strip() causes whitespace-only parameters to be returned (e.g. "   "), which will be truthy and can cause callers to treat a missing credential as present, potentially resulting in authentication bypass or incorrect authorization decisions.

Keeping leading/trailing whitespace in the returned parameter will make downstream token comparisons/validations fail (tokens will include extra spaces), breaking existing consumers that expect a trimmed credential value.

Replacing hasOwnProperty check with a truthiness check (flatErrors.nested![dotPath]) changes semantics: inherited properties will be treated as present and truthy values (e.g. functions from Object.prototype) may be accessed as if an array, causing runtime errors when .push is called.

Using the 'in' operator instead of hasOwnProperty changes semantics to include prototype properties and can throw a TypeError when value1 is null/undefined; this can cause incorrect merges of inherited properties or runtime exceptions.

Inlined $ref construction removed JSON Pointer escaping (replacing '~' with '~0' and '/' with '~1'), so referenceIds containing '~' or '/' will produce invalid or non-resolvable JSON Pointer fragments.
Second inlining of $ref construction also omits JSON Pointer escaping, causing the same invalid $ref issue for definition keys containing '~' or '/'.

Function now mutates the incoming value1 object in-place (value1[key] = ...) instead of returning a new merged object, breaking immutability and potentially causing caller-visible side effects and aliasing bugs.

In-place assignment into value1 (value1[index] = ...) can throw a TypeError if value1 (object or array) is non-extensible/sealed/frozen or has non-writable properties; previous copy-based approach avoided this.

If value1 and value2 are the same reference (or share nested references), merging in-place while iterating value2 may mutate the source during enumeration and produce incorrect/unstable merge behavior (skipped/duplicated keys or unexpected recursion).

Replacing Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(...) with Object.hasOwn(...) can break at runtime on older JS engines (older Node/browser versions) where Object.hasOwn is undefined, causing runtime errors.

Using Object.hasOwn requires TypeScript lib support (ES2022 / es2022.object); without the appropriate lib in tsconfig, compilation will fail with "Property 'hasOwn' does not exist on type 'ObjectConstructor'".

Switching from a type-only import to a runtime import of 'valibot' introduces a new runtime dependency that can break consumers or builds if 'valibot' is only a devDependency or not available at runtime.
Using // @ts-expect-error to silence type errors hides a potential mismatch between the local code and 'valibot' typings and may mask an actual incompatibility or missing export.

Calling v.getDefault(valibotSchema) assumes getDefault exists and has the same runtime semantics as the previous inline check; if the installed 'valibot' version lacks this export or differs, this will throw at runtime.

Replacing the simple typeof-function check with v.getDefault may change the resolved default value semantics (e.g., invocation context, argument passing, cloning), causing behavioral differences in produced JSON Schema.
Importing the entire 'valibot' namespace (import * as v) can negatively affect tree-shaking and bundle size compared with a named or type-only import.

Removing the outer non-capturing group changes alternation precedence so the pattern is effectively ^5[1-5]\d{2} OR (?:222\d|...|2720)\d{12}$ — the first alternative lacks a trailing $ and the second lacks a leading ^, allowing incorrect/partial matches and breaking Mastercard validation.

Returning the cached OutputDataset object by reference (instead of a shallow clone) allows downstream code to mutate the cached dataset, corrupting the cache and causing subsequent consumers to observe mutated/stale state.

Concurrent consumers (including multiple awaiters of the same in-flight run) now receive the same dataset object reference, so mutations by any consumer will affect others and the cached entry, creating race conditions and shared-mutation bugs.
defaultLogEntry.Panic now calls PrintPrettyStack(v) and no longer passes l.useColor, so it always prints colored output and ignores the logger's useColor setting.

prettyStack.parse hardcodes useColor := true (removing the parameter), preventing callers from disabling color and causing ANSI sequences to be emitted even when undesired (e.g., non-terminal outputs or log collectors).
Accessing the unexported routePattern field ties callers to internal representation and can break if the implementation changes; RoutePattern() encodes the public contract.
Adds an explicit increment of basicWriter.bytes after io.Copy even though basicWriter.Write (called by io.Copy) already updates the same counter, causing bytes to be double-counted.
Converts int64 n to int when adding to basicWriter.bytes (f.basicWriter.bytes += int(n)), which can overflow on 32-bit platforms or otherwise truncate large values.
Performs a separate non-atomic increment of basicWriter.bytes outside of basicWriter.Write, increasing the risk of a race or inconsistent counts if bytes is accessed concurrently.

Removing the early return causes next.ServeHTTP to be called and then fall through to the rest of the handler, which can result in next being invoked a second time (double response writes / corrupt response state) when hr is empty.

Replacing Header().Add("Vary", "Accept-Encoding") with Header().Set(...) will overwrite any existing Vary header values, potentially dropping other Vary directives set earlier by handlers or middleware instead of just ensuring Accept-Encoding is present and deduplicated.

Removed the wasm-target branch that used wasm_libc_shim and now unconditionally calls SystemTime::now(), which is known to panic or be unsupported on wasm targets (e.g. wasm64), reintroducing a runtime failure when building/running for wasm.

Removed postmaster/aux-process guard causes the postmaster to unconditionally remove SysV semaphore sets during on_shmem_exit, which will make subsequent crash-reinit child processes reference removed semaphore sets and likely fail (EINVAL) or abort startup.

Removed postmaster-only early return causes the postmaster to unconditionally munmap the master anonymous shared memory mapping during on_shmem_exit, which will leave re-forked children with unmapped addresses and cause SIGSEGV when they access shared structures.

Changing the allocation-limit error message from a specific wording to the generic "out of memory" is a behavioral API change that may break callers or monitoring that relied on the previous message text.
Replacing saturating_sub with plain subtraction in pq_getmsgbytes can underflow (and panic) if msg.cursor > msg.data.len(), introducing potential runtime panic or undefined behavior.
Replacing saturating_sub with plain subtraction in pq_copymsgbytes can underflow (and panic) if msg.cursor > msg.data.len(), making the function unsafe against malformed message state.
Replacing saturating_sub with plain subtraction in pq_getmsgtext can underflow (and panic) if msg.cursor > msg.data.len(), causing crashes when parsing malformed or unexpected input.

Removed snapshot/restore of CurrentResourceOwner around the internal subtransaction; after subtransaction release/rollback/unwind the CurrentResourceOwner can remain set to the parent TopTransaction owner causing outer-statement resource cleanup to target the wrong owner, leading to ResourceOwnerForgetRelationRef errors, rd_refcnt underflows and backend crashes.

Removed registration of the plpgsql exec seams that exposed CurrentResourceOwner get/set; code paths or third-party crates that relied on those seams being set at init may now fail to find the seam or behave differently.

Deleted the current_resource_owner/set_current_resource_owner seam declarations, removing the explicit API used previously to snapshot/restore the global CurrentResourceOwner and potentially breaking callers that expect to control CurrentResourceOwner manually.

Replacing wrapping_sub with plain u64 subtraction (write_rqst_ptr / XLOG_BLCKSZ as u64 - logwrt_result().Flush / XLOG_BLCKSZ as u64) can panic on underflow in debug builds when write_rqst_ptr < logwrt_result().Flush; the original used wrapping_sub to avoid that.

Behavioral change: previously the wrapped u64 delta was narrowed to a signed i32 producing a negative value when flush is past the request (causing no wakeup); the new code either panics (debug) or produces a large positive u64 on wrap (release), which will make the comparison flushblocks >= WalWriterFlushAfter true and cause spurious wakeups.

Casting wal_writer_flush_after to u64 for comparison (flushblocks >= wal_writer_flush_after as u64) changes semantics if WalWriterFlushAfter can be negative: a negative value becomes a large u64 and alters the comparison outcome compared to the original signed comparison.

Removing BlockSigAlarm from get_timeout_active allows a SIGALRM handler to call borrow_mut() while this function holds a RefCell borrow(), which can cause a RefCell already borrowed panic inside a signal handler and abort the process.

Removing BlockSigAlarm from get_timeout_indicator leaves a borrow_mut() unprotected against interruption by the SIGALRM handler, risking reentrant borrow conflicts that trigger a panic/abort or corrupt the indicator-reset semantics.

Removing BlockSigAlarm from get_timeout_start_time allows the SIGALRM handler to perform a borrow_mut() concurrent with this borrow(), risking a RefCell borrow error that will panic inside the signal handler and abort.

Removing BlockSigAlarm from get_timeout_finish_time removes protection against signal-handler reentrancy; concurrent borrow_mut() from the handler can cause a RefCell borrow panic inside the signal frame and abort the backend.

Removed error-context wrapping and the code that cleared plpgsql_context_attached, causing loss of PL/pgSQL-specific error context lines and leaving the 'attached once' latch uncleared which changes error propagation semantics for outer PL/pgSQL frames.

Dropping the bytes.remove(pos) step leaves a leading space before the substituted 'SELECT', changing the stored query text (" SELECT ..." instead of "SELECT ...") which may break callers or comparisons that expect the left-justified form.

Replacing clone_in(aexpr_clone_ctx(pstate)) with plain .clone() reintroduces the exact panic the comment warned about for Exprs that contain Query sublinks (plain Clone previously panicked for those cases).

clone_in used the parse-state clone context (aexpr_clone_ctx(pstate)) to ensure cloned Exprs use the correct memory/context; using the derived .clone() may allocate or preserve references in an incompatible context, leading to lifetime/ownership or memory-safety bugs.

Derived .clone() may be a shallow or different clone than clone_in produced (shared substructure/aliases), causing subtle aliasing/behavior differences when callers expect an independent deep copy of the SRF expression.

Removing the call to OldHeap.disarm_closer() means OldHeap's Drop will release the relcache reference even on success paths where cluster_rel_body already performed relation_close by OID, producing a double-release/double-close and likely crashing the backend.
Removing the public Relation::disarm_closer() method is an API-breaking change and will cause compilation errors in any other crates or callers that relied on this escape hatch.

effective_candidates() reads routes_version once and then writes self._effective_candidates and self._effective_candidates_version without re-checking, allowing a race where a concurrent router update can lead to the cache being overwritten with a stale version/content.

effective_low_priority_routes() uses a single initial read of routes_version and later assigns the rebuilt list and that initial version without re-checking, allowing a concurrent update to cause the cache to be reverted/overwritten with stale data.

Removed lock and replaced atomic assignment with in-place population for _effective_low_priority_routes, introducing the same race where callers may observe a partially-built list or concurrent mutations leading to exceptions or inconsistent results.
Removed unused 'threading' import — harmless if truly unused elsewhere, but ensure no other code relies on it.

Function calls get_route_path(scope) and inspects its final segment; get_route_path may return a route template (with path parameters) instead of the actual incoming request path, so this change can fail to detect asset requests and misclassify navigation requests.

Accept-header logic only treats exact '*/*' as a wildcard and ignores other wildcard patterns like 'text/*' (or other general types), which can lead to incorrect navigation detection for clients sending 'text/*' or other wildcard ranges.

If _iter_included_route_candidates yields tuples like (route, route_context) or other non-route objects, the code will call getattr on that tuple/object and won't extract the intended path/name, which can let an empty path slip past validation and allow invalid prefix+path combinations.

Replacing direct attribute access on specific route_context variants with getattr(r, ...) relaxes checks and can silently ignore missing attributes (path/name) that previously raised AttributeError, changing behavior and hiding errors.

The send stream may not be reliably closed when the producer task finishes (no async-with or explicit aclose for send_stream), which can prevent receive_stream from ever getting EndOfStream and cause the consumer/task group to hang or leak.

Removal of the async_exit_stack enter/push_async_callback logic means stream cleanup is now dependent on async generator cleanup rather than the request-scoped exit stack, increasing the chance of ResourceWarning or unclean shutdown when the response stops early.
send_stream (the producer-side memory stream) is created but never closed (no async with/send_stream.aclose), risking leaking the send stream and ResourceWarnings.

Removed the local GenerateJsonSchema subclass that provided a bytes_schema override (and a compatibility workaround), which can break FastAPI when running against older supported pydantic versions that required that override.

Changing UploadFile's JSON schema from {type:string, contentMediaType:application/octet-stream} to {type:string, format:binary} is a breaking schema change for consumers that relied on contentMediaType to detect file MIME information.

Removed custom GenerateJsonSchema.bytes_schema override that added contentEncoding (e.g., base64) based on pydantic config, so JSON schema for bytes may lose contentEncoding information and change behavior for byte fields elsewhere.

Converting on_startup/on_shutdown to lists earlier in __init__ will eagerly consume any iterables/generators passed in, changing the timing of their side effects and exceptions (now occurring before prefix validation and other initialization).

Removing the Json special-case causes sequence fields annotated with pydantic.Json (or Json present in field_info.metadata) to be pulled with values.getlist instead of values.get, breaking handling of JSON arrays provided as a single form/query/header value and changing request parsing semantics.

On Python >=3.14, removing the annotation_format=Format.FORWARDREF fallback causes inspect.signature(call) to attempt to re-evaluate TYPE_CHECKING-only annotations and can re-raise NameError (previously avoided), leading to unhandled exceptions.
Removing param.strip() returns parameter with any leading/trailing whitespace (e.g. multiple spaces after scheme), changing function semantics and likely breaking callers that expect a trimmed token.

Replacing an own-property check with direct property access allows special keys (e.g. "__proto__"/"constructor") to resolve to prototype properties and may cause prototype mutation or runtime TypeErrors when code attempts to .push on inherited values.

Using the `in` operator instead of hasOwnProperty lets inherited properties from the prototype chain be treated as present, causing unexpected merges into/involving prototype properties and altering application semantics (and opening prototype-related risks).

If value1 and value2 are the same reference (self-merge), mutating value1 while iterating value2 can alter enumeration/iteration behavior and produce incorrect or inconsistent merge results.

The object-merge branch now mutates the incoming value1 in-place instead of producing a new merged object, changing observable behavior and introducing unintended side-effects for callers that expect immutability.
The array-merge branch mutates value1 in-place, which can corrupt merge semantics when value1 and value2 share nested references or when recursion relies on unmodified originals.

Writing directly to value1 (properties and array indices) will throw TypeError at runtime if value1 is non-writable, non-extensible, sealed, or frozen (or if its properties are non-writable), whereas the previous copy-based approach avoided those failures.

The async generator now yields from inside `async with anyio.create_task_group()`, so if the response iterator is not exhausted (e.g. client disconnect / cancellation), finalization throws GeneratorExit at the yield and the task group's cancel scope is exited during asyncgen finalization — typically in a different task than it was entered in — raising RuntimeError ("Attempted to exit cancel scope in a different task") and/or leaving the producer task and memory streams un-cleaned; this is precisely the PEP 789 problem the removed AsyncExitStack-based context manager was designed to avoid.

FastAPI emits OpenAPI 3.1.0 documents, where `format: binary` is not a defined/valid representation for binary payloads (it was removed in 3.1 in favor of `contentMediaType`), so file upload schemas become spec-invalid for the generated OpenAPI version.

Removing the Json-field exclusion makes sequence-typed Json parameters (e.g. `Query(...)` annotated `Json[List[int]]`) resolve via `getlist`, so the JSON-encoded string is wrapped in a list and Json validation fails with a 422 instead of parsing the payload.

On Python 3.14+ the fallback `inspect.signature(call)` still evaluates annotations (Format.VALUE by default), so it re-raises the same NameError the except block is meant to recover from, breaking dependencies with TYPE_CHECKING-only annotations.

Removing `.strip()` is not redundant: `partition(" ")` only splits on the first space, so extra leading spaces (e.g. "Bearer  token") or trailing whitespace/CR characters remain in the returned credential, breaking token comparison and Basic-auth base64 decoding.

Using plain property access instead of hasOwnProperty resolves inherited Object.prototype members, so a dot path like "constructor", "toString" or "valueOf" is treated as already present and `.push` is called on a function, throwing a TypeError.

`key in value1` also matches prototype-chain properties, so keys such as "toString" or "constructor" present on value2 are merged against inherited functions of value1, producing spurious merge issues instead of copying the value2 entry.
Inlining the template drops the JSON Pointer escaping (`~` -> `~0`, `/` -> `~1`), producing invalid/incorrect `$ref` values for definition keys containing `/` or `~`.
Same missing JSON Pointer escaping at the second `$ref` construction site, so references to definitions with special characters no longer resolve.

Merging now mutates `value1` in place instead of a copy, so the object returned by the first schema (which for schemas like `any`, `unknown`, `custom`, `instance`, or `looseObject` passthrough can be the caller's original input object) is destructively modified, producing unexpected side effects for callers.
Array branch writes merged items directly into `value1`, mutating the caller-provided/first-schema array instead of returning a fresh array.
On the failure path the function returns early after already having mutated some entries of `value1`, leaving the input partially merged/corrupted even though the merge is reported as unsuccessful.

Removing the outer non-capturing group makes `|` split the whole pattern, so the first alternative `^5[1-5]\d{2}` matches any string merely starting with 51-55 (no 12-digit suffix, no `$`), accepting invalid card numbers like "5111" or "5112abc".
The second alternative `(?:222\d|...)\d{12}$` lost the `^` anchor, so it matches a valid Mastercard prefix anywhere in the input (e.g. "xx2221..."), allowing malformed values to pass validation.

Returning the cached dataset object by reference lets downstream pipe items mutate it (e.g. pushing into `issues` via `_addIssue` or reassigning `value`/`typed`), permanently corrupting the cache entry for all subsequent hits.
Cache hit now returns the stored dataset instance directly, so any downstream mutation of `issues`/`value` corrupts the cached entry and leaks state across validation runs.

The same dataset object is both stored in the cache and returned to every concurrent awaiter of the shared in-flight promise, so mutations by one caller's downstream pipe items are observed by other callers and by future cache hits.

Panic now calls PrintPrettyStack, which hardcodes color output, so ANSI escape codes are emitted even when the log entry was configured with useColor=false (e.g. non-TTY output or Windows), regressing plain-text panic logs.

rctx.routePattern only holds the pattern matched in the current mux's tree, whereas RoutePattern() joins rctx.RoutePatterns across mounted subrouters and normalizes wildcards/trailing slashes, so r.Pattern will now lose the mount prefix (and wildcard/trailing-slash cleanup) for nested routers.
io.Copy goes through basicWriter.Write which already increments basicWriter.bytes, so the added `f.basicWriter.bytes += int(n)` double-counts the bytes written in the tee'd path.

Removing the return causes next.ServeHTTP to be invoked twice when the router has no routes (once in the empty-router branch and again at the fallthrough no-match path), producing duplicated response bodies and 'superfluous WriteHeader' errors.

Removing the wasm branch makes timeofday() rely on std::time::SystemTime::now(), which panics (rather than reading the host clock) if the crate is ever compiled for a wasm target, and likely leaves the wasm_libc_shim dependency unused.

Removing the postmaster guard makes release_semaphores IPC_RMID the shared SysV semaphore sets during crash reinit's shmem_exit(1) in the postmaster, so re-forked children's PGSemaphoreReset hits a removed set and fails with EINVAL, aborting startup.

Removing the postmaster guard makes anonymous_shmem_detach munmap the postmaster's master anonymous shared segment during crash reinit (which deliberately skips re-creating it), leaving re-forked children with dangling shared-memory pointers and a SIGSEGV on first touch.

Removing the `oldowner = CurrentResourceOwner` snapshot before `BeginInternalSubTransaction` drops behavior pl_exec.c requires: subxact cleanup leaves `CurrentResourceOwner` at the parent (CurTransaction) owner rather than the portal owner the block ran under, so the outer statement's relation refs/buffer pins are later forgotten under the wrong owner (refcount underflow / backend crash).

On the no-error path, `release_current_subtransaction` leaves `CurrentResourceOwner` set to the parent owner and it is no longer restored to the caller's (portal) owner, corrupting subsequent resource-owner accounting for the enclosing statement.

Both error paths (panic re-raise and the PG_CATCH handler path) now run after rollback without restoring `CurrentResourceOwner`, so EXCEPTION handler statements and the unwinding outer statement's resowner cleanup execute against the wrong resource owner.

Plain u64 subtraction underflows when LogwrtResult.Flush is already ahead of write_rqst_ptr, panicking in debug builds and wrapping to a huge value in release builds, which then always exceeds WalWriterFlushAfter and triggers spurious WAL writer wakeups (the removed wrapping/i32 code deliberately produced a negative value that failed the test).

Removing the BlockSigAlarm guard lets an interrupting SIGALRM handler call borrow_mut() while this bare borrow() is live, causing a 'RefCell already borrowed' panic inside a non-unwinding signal frame that aborts the backend.
get_timeout_indicator now takes a borrow_mut() without blocking SIGALRM, so a signal-handler reentrant borrow_mut() panics (or the handler's mutation is lost), aborting the process.
get_timeout_start_time's bare borrow() is no longer protected against SIGALRM reentrancy, risking a RefCell double-borrow panic in the signal handler.
get_timeout_finish_time's bare borrow() is no longer protected against SIGALRM reentrancy, risking a RefCell double-borrow panic in the signal handler.

Dropping the SPI error-context wrapper means errors escaping an embedded query no longer carry the `SQL statement "..."` / `PL/pgSQL expression "..."` / `PL/pgSQL assignment "..."` context line, silently degrading error reporting at this boundary.

Removing the reset of `plpgsql_context_attached = false` leaves the "attached once" latch set when crossing the SPI boundary, so an outer PL/pgSQL frame can no longer attach its own function context line to the propagating error.

Dropping `bytes.remove(pos)` leaves the substituted query text as " SELECT ..." instead of "SELECT ...", so the stored/reported PERFORM expression text (used in error messages and any text comparisons/caching keys) gains a spurious leading space and diverges from upstream behavior.

Replacing the clone_in/copyObject deep-copy with the derived .clone() reintroduces the documented panic when the SRF's argument list embeds a SubLink with an owned Query subselect (e.g. ts_debug's `ts_parse((SELECT cfgparser ...), $2)`).

The derived Clone likely does not allocate nested nodes in the parse-state arena (aexpr_clone_ctx), so the returned Expr<'mcx> may hold copies with different ownership/allocation semantics than the rest of the parse tree, risking lifetime/arena inconsistency.

Removing the disarm_closer call re-introduces a double release of OldHeap's relcache reference: cluster_rel_body already performs the C-level relation_close by OID on every Ok path, so the owned Relation handle's Drop will now release the refcount a second time and trip the rd_refcnt > 0 assertion (VACUUM FULL / CLUSTER backend crash).

Deleting Relation::disarm_closer removes the only mechanism for transferring close ownership away from the RAII handle, leaving no safe way to model paths where the relation is closed by OID elsewhere.

Removing the lock and building the cache in place on `self._effective_candidates` means two concurrent rebuilds can interleave: each thread resets the attribute to a fresh list while the other is still appending, so the final `return self._effective_candidates` can hand back a partially populated route list (leading to missing routes/404s).

Same in-place rebuild race in `effective_low_priority_routes`: concurrent invocations reset and append to the shared `self._effective_low_priority_routes` attribute, so the returned list may be incomplete or contain another thread's partial results.
`os.path.splitext` is used but the diff does not add an `import os`, which will raise NameError at request time if `os` is not already imported in this module.

Treating any path whose last segment contains a dot as a non-navigation request breaks legitimate SPA deep links (e.g. /users/john.doe, /docs/v1.2, /items/2024.report), and this check short-circuits even when the client explicitly sends `Accept: text/html`.

Accepting `*/*` as a navigation signal makes non-browser clients (curl, fetch, XHR without Accept overrides) receive the HTML shell instead of a 404/API response, since `*/*` is their default Accept value.
Range wildcards such as `text/*` are still not recognized, so a client sending only `Accept: text/*` is not detected as a navigation request even though it accepts text/html.

The loop now calls `_iter_included_route_candidates`, but no such helper is introduced or imported in this change (only `_iter_routes_with_context` existed), so `include_router` will raise NameError at runtime whenever a prefix-less router is included.

The async generator now yields from inside `anyio.create_task_group()` (and the `receive_stream` context), so the task group's cancel scope is exited during generator finalization rather than by structured teardown — this is the PEP 789 hazard the removed `AsyncExitStack`/context-manager wiring existed to avoid and can raise "Attempted to exit cancel scope in a different task than it was entered in" / leave the producer task and memory streams uncleaned when the client disconnects or the generator is closed/GC'd from another task.

Deleting the GenerateJsonSchema subclass changes the JSON schema for every plain `bytes` field (not just UploadFile), reverting them to pydantic's default (`format: base64url`/`binary`) and silently altering generated OpenAPI for unrelated models.

`{"type": "string", "format": "binary"}` is the OpenAPI 3.0 convention and is not valid/meaningful in the JSON Schema dialect used by OpenAPI 3.1 (FastAPI's default output), where `contentMediaType` is the correct keyword.

self.on_startup/self.on_shutdown are now assigned before super().__init__() runs, so if Starlette's Router.__init__ still initializes these attributes (older/compatible Starlette versions), the user-provided handlers would be silently overwritten with empty lists; previously the assignment after super() guaranteed FastAPI's values won.

Dropping the Json-field exclusion means a Json-annotated query/header/form field whose parsed type is a sequence (e.g. `Query(Json)` with `List[...]`) now reads via `getlist`, wrapping the raw JSON string in a list (`['[1,2]']`) so JSON decoding/validation fails instead of parsing the single string value.

Dropping the Json-field exclusion means Json-annotated sequence fields (e.g. Query(Json[List[int]])) now read via getlist, yielding a list of raw strings instead of the single JSON string that needs parsing, causing validation errors.

On Python 3.14+ the fallback `inspect.signature(call)` defaults to Format.VALUE and will eagerly evaluate annotations, so it raises the same NameError the except block is meant to recover from, breaking dependencies with TYPE_CHECKING-only annotations.

Dropping .strip() is not redundant: str.partition only splits at the first space, so any additional leading whitespace (e.g. "Bearer  token") or trailing CR/LF/spaces is now returned as part of the credential, which will break token comparison/JWT decoding for such headers.

Replacing the own-property check with a truthiness lookup makes inherited Object.prototype keys (e.g. a dot path of "constructor", "toString", "valueOf") appear present, so `.push` is called on a prototype function and throws a TypeError instead of creating a new array.

Using `in` instead of hasOwnProperty also matches inherited prototype keys, so a key only present on value2 but named like a prototype member (e.g. "toString", "constructor") is wrongly treated as shared and deep-merged against the prototype value, producing a spurious merge failure.
Inlining the template drops the JSON Pointer escaping (`~` -> `~0`, `/` -> `~1`), so definition keys containing those characters now produce invalid/mis-resolving `$ref` values.
Same loss of JSON Pointer escaping here; the emitted `$ref` will not match the `$defs` key when the reference id contains `~` or `/`.
The array branch now writes merged items directly into `value1`, mutating the caller's array instead of producing a new one.

When a nested `_merge` returns an issue and the function returns early, `value1` has already been partially overwritten, leaving the input object/array in a corrupted half-merged state that is observable to the caller.

Writing merged entries directly onto `value1` mutates the first schema's output object in place, which can be the caller's original input (e.g. when a branch schema such as `any`, `unknown`, `custom` or `instance` returns the input by reference), causing unexpected side effects on user data.
The array branch now assigns merged items into `value1` in place (and leaves it partially mutated on an early issue return), mutating a possibly shared/input array rather than producing a new one.

Object.hasOwn is ES2022-only, so this drops support for older runtimes (e.g. Node < 16.9, older browsers) that the previous Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call form worked on, and will fail type-checking unless the tsconfig `lib` includes ES2022.Object.

The bare `// @ts-expect-error` (no description) blanket-suppresses every type error on the `v.getDefault(valibotSchema)` line, hiding genuine mismatches (e.g. passing a schema variant without a `default`) and it will itself become a compile error if valibot's overloads ever accept this call.
Second bare `// @ts-expect-error` suppression has the same problem: it masks all type errors on the call and breaks the build if the error stops occurring.

Changing `import type * as v from 'valibot'` to a value import introduces a hard runtime dependency on valibot in this module (previously type-only), pulling the library into the bundle and requiring valibot to be resolvable at runtime rather than only as a type-level peer.

Removing the outer non-capturing group makes `|` split the whole pattern, so the first alternative `^5[1-5]\d{2}` matches any string starting with 51–55 plus two digits (no length/end anchor) and the second alternative loses the `^` anchor, causing invalid card numbers to be accepted.

Returning the cached dataset object by reference lets downstream pipe items (which mutate `dataset.value`/push into `dataset.issues` in place) corrupt the cached entry, so subsequent cache hits return mutated values and accumulated issues.
Cache hit now returns the stored dataset by reference; any in-place mutation by downstream pipe items or by the caller permanently poisons the cached dataset shared across all future runs.

The same dataset instance is both stored in the cache and returned (and shared with all concurrent callers awaiting the deduplicated promise), so mutations by one consumer leak into the cache and into other concurrent callers' results.
Panic now always prints ANSI-colored stack output, ignoring the log entry's useColor setting, so panic traces emit escape codes when color is disabled (non-TTY/Windows).
Hardcoding useColor := true removes the ability for callers to disable colorization, making the local variable a dead configuration point.

rctx.routePattern only holds the pattern matched by the current (sub-)router, whereas RoutePattern() joins RoutePatterns across the whole router stack and normalizes wildcards/trailing slashes, so r.Pattern becomes wrong (e.g. only the leaf segment) for mounted/sub-router routes.
io.Copy into &f.basicWriter already invokes basicWriter.Write, which increments basicWriter.bytes, so the added `f.basicWriter.bytes += int(n)` double-counts the bytes written.
io.Copy into &f.basicWriter already increments basicWriter.bytes via Write, so the added `f.basicWriter.bytes += int(n)` double-counts the bytes written in the tee'd ReadFrom path.

Removing the `return` makes the empty-router case fall through to the loop and the trailing `next.ServeHTTP(w, r)`, so the downstream handler is invoked twice (duplicate response body, "superfluous WriteHeader" errors, possible double side effects) whenever HeaderRouter is empty.

Using Set instead of Add overwrites any Vary values already set by the handler or upstream middleware (e.g. Origin, Cookie, Accept), which can break content negotiation and cause cache poisoning; the duplicate-value concern should instead be handled by checking for an existing Accept-Encoding entry (WriteHeader is already guarded against multiple invocations).

Removing the wasm-specific clock path means any future/incidental wasm build of this crate will panic inside SystemTime::now() instead of reading the host clock, silently reintroducing the bug the cfg branch guarded against.

Removing the postmaster guard makes crash reinit's shmem_exit(1) in the postmaster semctl(IPC_RMID) the persistent SysV semaphore sets that re-forked children still reference, so the next child's PGSemaphoreReset will fail with EINVAL since this tree never re-runs PGReserveSemaphores.

Dropping the postmaster guard lets the postmaster munmap its master anonymous shared segment during crash reinit, and since this tree deliberately skips re-creating shared memory, re-forked children inherit an unmapped address space and will SIGSEGV on first access to shared structures.

Replacing `saturating_sub` with plain `msg.data.len() - msg.cursor` removes the guard against a cursor past the end of the buffer: if that invariant is ever broken (cursor is externally settable on StringInfo), this panics on subtraction overflow in debug and wraps to a huge value in release, letting the insufficient-data check pass and causing a slice panic instead of a protocol-violation error.

Same unchecked subtraction in `pq_copymsgbytes`: `msg.data.len() - msg.cursor` can underflow/panic when cursor exceeds the data length, whereas `saturating_sub` previously produced the clean protocol-violation error.
Same unchecked subtraction in `pq_getmsgtext`: overflow of `msg.data.len() - msg.cursor` turns a recoverable error path into a panic (debug) or wrapped comparison plus out-of-range slicing (release).

Changing the errmsg to "out of memory" diverges from the PG 18.3 wording the crate mirrors ("string buffer exceeds maximum allowed length (%zu bytes)"), so client-visible error text no longer matches upstream stringinfo.c.

Dropping the `oldowner = CurrentResourceOwner` snapshot before `BeginInternalSubTransaction` removes the only record of the portal's resource owner, so nothing can restore it after the subxact engine leaves `CurrentResourceOwner` pointing at the parent (CurTransaction) owner.

On the panic/unwind path the subtransaction rollback leaves `CurrentResourceOwner` at the parent owner, so the unwinding outer statement's cleanup forgets relation refs/buffer pins under the wrong owner (ResourceOwnerForgetRelationRef failure and rd_refcnt underflow).

After `ReleaseCurrentSubTransaction` / `RollbackAndReleaseCurrentSubTransaction` the code no longer restores the caller's resource owner, so subsequent block/EXCEPTION-handler statements and the outer statement's resowner cleanup run under the parent owner instead of the portal owner that opened those resources.
On the panic-unwind path the rollback no longer restores the saved resource owner, so unwinding outer-statement resowner cleanup runs against the parent owner and can abort the backend.

Plain u64 subtraction underflows when the flush position is already past the requested async LSN (a common case), panicking in debug builds and wrapping to a huge value in release builds that always satisfies the >= threshold and triggers spurious WAL writer wakeups.
Casting the signed WalWriterFlushAfter GUC to u64 turns any negative value into an enormous unsigned threshold, suppressing wakeups instead of the previous signed comparison semantics.

Removing the BlockSigAlarm guard lets a SIGALRM-interrupting handle_sig_alarm() call borrow_mut() while this bare borrow() is live, causing a 'RefCell already borrowed' panic inside a non-unwinding C signal frame that aborts the backend.

get_timeout_indicator holds a borrow_mut() with SIGALRM unblocked, so a signal delivered mid-borrow makes the handler's borrow_mut() panic (and mutate/observe partially updated indicator state), aborting the process.
Dropping BlockSigAlarm from get_timeout_start_time reintroduces the RefCell reentrancy abort when SIGALRM arrives during the borrow.
Dropping BlockSigAlarm from get_timeout_finish_time reintroduces the RefCell reentrancy abort when SIGALRM arrives during the borrow.

Removing `bytes.remove(pos)` leaves the injected leading space in the rewritten query, so PERFORM statements are stored as " SELECT ..." instead of "SELECT ...", changing the query text reported in error messages/plan caches (and duplicating whitespace when pos > 0).

Removing `bytes.remove(pos)` leaves the extra leading space introduced by substituting " SELECT" for "PERFORM", so the rewritten query text is " SELECT ..." instead of "SELECT ...", changing stored/reported expression text (and breaking any exact-match expectations on it).

Replacing the deliberate `clone_in`/copyObject path with the derived `.clone()` reintroduces the documented panic when the SRF's argument list embeds a `SubLink` with an owned `Query` subselect (e.g. `ts_parse((SELECT cfgparser ...), $2)`), so `transformCallStmt`/ts_debug-style queries will abort instead of copying the node.

Dropping the disarm call means that on the success path, where cluster_rel_body has already released OldHeap's relcache reference by OID, the owned Relation handle's Drop will release it a second time, tripping the rd_refcnt > 0 assertion and crashing the backend on CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL.

Removing `Relation::disarm_closer` eliminates the only supported way to transfer close ownership away from an owned handle, leaving any code path where the relation is closed by OID with no way to avoid a double-close.

Removing the lock and double-checked version guard allows concurrent rebuilds; two threads mutating self._effective_candidates in place (reset to [] mid-build by another thread, interleaved appends) can produce a partial or duplicated candidate list that is then permanently cached once the version stamp is set.

Building the cache by mutating the shared instance attribute self._effective_candidates instead of a local list (as the old code did) exposes a partially populated list to any code that reads the attribute directly during the rebuild.

effective_low_priority_routes has the same unsynchronized in-place rebuild of self._effective_low_priority_routes, so concurrent callers can corrupt the list and stamp the corrupted result with the current routes version, caching it indefinitely.

The diff introduces calls to os.path.splitext and get_route_path without adding corresponding imports; if `os` and `get_route_path` are not already imported in fastapi/routing.py this raises NameError on every request hitting this code path.

os.path.splitext treats any dot in the final path segment as an extension, so version- or dotted-segment routes like /api/v1.0 or /users/john.doe are misclassified as asset requests and excluded from navigation handling.

The extension check runs before the Accept header is inspected, so a genuine browser navigation to an .html path (e.g. /index.html) now returns False, changing prior behavior where an html-accepting request was treated as navigation.
Treating a bare `*/*` Accept as navigation misclassifies programmatic clients (curl, fetch/XHR, and many SDKs default to `Accept: */*`), which will now receive frontend HTML instead of API responses.
Only exact `*/*` is considered a wildcard; `text/*` with nonzero quality is still ignored, so requests explicitly accepting any text type are not treated as navigation while the broader `*/*` is.

Yielding from inside an anyio task group (a cancel scope) in an async generator reintroduces the PEP 789 hazard the removed exit-stack wiring explicitly avoided: when the consumer stops early (e.g., client disconnect), GeneratorExit is thrown at the yield and the task group's __aexit__ runs during aclose()/GC finalization, which can execute in a different task and raise RuntimeError ('Attempted to exit cancel scope in a different task' / 'async generator ignored GeneratorExit').

The explicit `tg.cancel_scope.cancel()` from the old code was dropped, so on early generator termination the producer task is never cancelled: closing receive_stream makes the producer raise BrokenResourceError (which replaces GeneratorExit and escapes as an exception group), and if the producer is blocked awaiting the user's generator the task group __aexit__ waits indefinitely, hanging finalization.

Cleanup now depends on async-generator finalization (StreamingResponse or GC calling aclose) instead of the request-scoped AsyncExitStack; if the generator is abandoned without prompt aclose, the producer task, memory streams, and the user's SSE generator leak until event-loop asyncgen shutdown, and the removed `receive_stream.aclose` push no longer guards against ResourceWarning.
